I am 63 years old now, and my bones ache when the weather turns. I have been farming this land in Quzhou since I was a young bride, and I never went to school — my hands know more than any book. My family has about 12 mu of land, and my husband passed away years ago, so I mostly decide things myself, though my son helps when the machines are needed.

This year, I will stick to what I know and what my body can still manage. I will grow **winter wheat** and **summer maize** in rotation on 10 mu of my best land. Everyone in our village does this — it is the safest way to fill our bellies and sell the surplus. I thought about planting cotton on a small plot for extra cash, but at my age, all the spraying and hand-picking is too hard. Cotton needs medicine almost every week, and my back cannot bend like that anymore. Wheat and maize are easier because the machines do most of the work now, and the county grain station buys them reliably.

For the wheat, I will use improved seeds — the kind called *jimai* or *lumai* that the seed shop sells. I will rotary till the soil before sowing in early October. I will put down compound fertilizer as basal dressing and topdress with urea in spring. The wheat needs three irrigations: one before winter, one at green-up, and one at heading. I will spray pesticide about four times when the aphids and rust come.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will plant hybrid maize — *denghai605* is what most people use here. We sow directly into the wheat stubble with no-tillage now; there is no need to plough again. The maize needs less fertilizer than wheat, and two irrigations are usually enough if the summer rains are kind. I will spray pesticide four times for the corn borers and weeds.

I will keep 2 mu of my land fallow or let my neighbor use it for vegetables in exchange for some help. I do not have the strength to manage more crops than wheat and maize.
